newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Asian currencies firm as Malaysia gets tough.
newsitem.headline: Asian currencies firm as Malaysia gets tough.

text.p: Asian currencies received a boost on Monday after Malaysia squared up and came out fighting against speculators by limiting non-trade swap transactions.
The ringgit rallied to 2.5800 per U.S. dollar from Friday's late level of around 2.6350 and while the scale of the rise was not mirrored elsewhere, Asian currencies were generally firmer.
The Malaysian central bank, Bank Negara, announced on Sunday that from Monday, local banks will have to limit non-trade related currency swaps with overseas customers to $2.0 million.
A swap is a forward rate agreement to exchange one currency for another. By imposing a $2.0 million ceiling, overseas players will be limited on the amount of ringgit they can get hold of.
As they stand, the controls are somewhat mild in nature and after much tough talking from Prime Minister Mahathir Mohamad against currency speculators they came a little surprise.

"I don't think this move in itself have too much impact but what people are worried about is that it could put Malaysia a step back in terms of trying to be a financial centre," said Chaing Yao Chye, head of Asia Pacific research at CIBC in Singapore.
Analysts doubted much of a squeeze would result from the move as offshore players are not too short of ringgit.
They said most had learned from the Thai experience, where shortsellers of baht were left stranded when their supply of the currency was cut off by capital controls imposed by the government.

This meant that in the last couple of months, players had actually borrowed in the swap market before they sold the ringgit off, although analysts said there will be upward pressure on offshore forward rates because of the move.
"I don't think it's Bank Negara's aim to squeeze the offshore market the way Thailand did. This is more to prevent people getting cheap ringgit offshore to put on new positions," CIBC's Chaing said.

The news boosted regional currencies, with the Singapore dollar up at 1.4580 per U.S. dollar from Friday's 1.4750, the Indonesia rupiah up at 2,592.0 from 2.610.0 and the onshore baht up slightly at 31.700 from 31.900.

The move by Malaysia is similar to the Singapore system whereby a swap involving a forward sale of U.S. dollar/Singapore dollar to non-residents requires offical approval if the amount exceeds 5.0 million Singapore dollars and the transaction is unrelated to trade.
So apart from Singapore and the Philippines, where controls already exist, could this happen anywhere else in Southeast Asia? The answer would seem to be no.
There is much speculation that Thailand will in fact lift existing capital controls as part of the International Monetary Fund (IMF) sponsored economic package due this week.
In Indonesia, no end is in sight to the liberal exchange rate system.

"Indonesia has a policy to liberalise exchange controls as much as they can and they have already widened the intervention band," said one trader at a European bank in Singapore. "President Suharto has made it pretty clear that he is happy with the liberal system that's in place for the rupiah."
While Malaysia's move was fairly mild and was good news for the ringgit, it hammered the stock market, with Malaysian blue chip stocks diving 4.5 percent in early trading.
"It's not the actual control they have put in place which is worrying investors, it's the fact they have done it at all," said one Singapore based analyst.
"If you keep changing the rules you are bound to put people off, you can't do things like this and not expect people to worry that there are toughter measures to come."
-- Singapore newsroom (+65-870-3080)
